national.title: Medical cannabis under a state license is now Schedule III
national.text: A federal final rule dated April 28, 2026 placed FDA-approved marijuana products and medical marijuana products regulated by a state medical marijuana license in Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act. The rule names medical products, not adult-use products. A separate proceeding on moving marijuana generally from Schedule I to Schedule III had a hearing set for June 29 to July 15, 2026; the DEA page reports no decision.

national.title: NORML state-by-state guide to laws and penalties
national.text: NORML (the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws), an advocacy group, keeps pages on cannabis laws and penalties for every state, DC and federal law. It says the pages are not legal advice and suggests checking state statutes or an attorney.

national.title: Flying with cannabis
national.text: TSA says marijuana and certain cannabis products, including some CBD oil, remain illegal under federal law unless they contain no more than 0.3 percent THC on a dry-weight basis or are FDA-approved. Screeners do not search for drugs, but they refer any they find to law enforcement.

national.title: Medical cannabis patient travel guide
national.text: Americans for Safe Access, a medical cannabis patient advocacy group, publishes a guide for patients traveling between states: state-by-state laws, patients’ rights and where medical cannabis can be obtained. The page says it was last updated in December 2024.

national.title: VA care and state cannabis programs
national.text: Taking part in a state marijuana program does not affect eligibility for VA care, and veterans will not be denied VA benefits because of marijuana use. VA providers discuss marijuana use as part of care, but VA clinicians may not recommend medical marijuana or complete state program forms.

national.title: Find free civil legal aid
national.text: The Legal Services Corporation’s tool finds a local legal aid organization by address or city and links to LawHelp.org for legal information and forms. LSC-funded programs serve low-income people with civil legal problems.

national.title: Which states seal records automatically
national.text: The Clean Slate Initiative, an advocacy organization for automatic record sealing, lists the states and DC whose laws meet its criteria (14 states and DC on November 15, 2026), with links to each state campaign.

national.title: 50-state comparison of record relief
national.text: The Collateral Consequences Resource Center compares expungement, sealing and other record relief across all 50 states and DC, with a summary for each state. The page says it was updated in July 2024. Read it on the center’s site.

national.title: Find your state legislators by address
national.text: Open States, now run by Plural, looks up your state legislators from an address or your current location. Its page notes an exception for Montana while that state finishes redistricting.

national.title: Poison Help: 1-800-222-1222
national.text: A free poison help line, open 24 hours a day in over 100 languages, run by the federal Health Resources and Services Administration.

national.title: SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357
national.text: Free, confidential treatment referral and information for mental health and substance use, 24 hours a day, in English and Spanish.

national.title: National Cannabis Industry Association
national.text: A national trade association for the legal cannabis industry. Its members include state-licensed cannabis companies, hemp manufacturers and service providers, and it advocates for national policy changes.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: State law (AS 17.38) makes marijuana use legal only for people 21 and older. An adult may possess up to 1 ounce for personal use.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs (AS 17.38)

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Marijuana may be bought only from licensed retail marijuana stores. Delivery is not allowed.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: It is a crime to drive while impaired by marijuana.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Employers may restrict employees’ marijuana use
answers.detail: Alaska’s marijuana law says nothing in it requires an employer to permit or accommodate the use, possession or growing of marijuana in the workplace, or affects an employer’s ability to have policies restricting marijuana use by employees. Employers and others who control private property may also prohibit marijuana on it. This is the Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office’s copy of the chapter as of July 25, 2018, which is marked as not an official copy.

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: Up to 12 plants per home, 6 mature
answers.detail: No more than 12 plants, with six or fewer mature and flowering, may be present in a single dwelling.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Medical cards are issued under AS 17.37. The adult-use law did not change their privileges or prohibitions.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs (AS 17.37)

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: An adult 21 or older may possess up to 1 ounce of marijuana for personal use.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: Not in public; some stores allow on-site use
answers.detail: Using marijuana in public is illegal. Some licensed retail stores hold an on-site consumption endorsement that allows use there.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: An adult 21 or older may give 1 ounce or less to another adult 21 or older. Buying or selling it outside licensed stores is not allowed.
answers.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Alabama has no adult-use law. A first offense of possessing marijuana for personal use is a Class A misdemeanor. That is existing law as summarized in a February 2026 Senate bill; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Code of Ala. 13A-12-214, per the 2026 Senate Bill 285 synopsis; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission runs the state’s medical cannabis program for patients and caregivers. Whether licensed dispensaries are open is not yet reviewed.
answers.citation: Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Arkansas has no adult-use law. Possessing less than 4 ounces of marijuana is a Class A misdemeanor. That is the law as the Arkansas Sentencing Commission quoted it in 2019; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Ark. Code 5-64-419(b)(5)(A), per the Arkansas Sentencing Commission (2019); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Arkansas’s constitution as barring employers from discriminating against qualifying patients and caregivers in hiring, firing or the terms of employment. Its chart says the amendment still lets employers take listed actions and points to the amendment for the full limits. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Ark. Const. amend. 98, § 3, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Arkansas Department of Health issues medical marijuana registry cards. A separate state agency licenses dispensaries.
answers.citation: Arkansas Department of Health, Medical marijuana

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: An adult 21 or older may possess and use 1 ounce or less of marijuana, of which no more than 5 grams may be concentrate.

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Licensed marijuana establishments may sell to consumers, up to 1 ounce per transaction, no more than 5 grams of it concentrate.

answers.question: driving
answers.short: No driving impaired to the slightest degree
answers.detail: The law does not allow driving while impaired to even the slightest degree by marijuana, or consuming it while driving or riding in a vehicle. Metabolites in a driver’s system count toward an impaired-driving charge only if the driver is impaired to the slightest degree.

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Arizona as barring employers from refusing to hire, firing or penalizing a registered patient for that status or for a positive marijuana test, unless the person used or was impaired by marijuana at work. Its chart lists an exception where the employer would lose a federal benefit. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: A.R.S. § 36-2813, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Plants must be at the adult’s primary residence, in an enclosed area with a lock that keeps out minors and not visible from public view. No more than 12 plants at a residence with two or more adults.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Arizona Department of Health Services licenses the medical marijuana program for qualifying patients, caregivers and dispensaries.
answers.citation: Arizona Department of Health Services, Marijuana licensing

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: No more than 5 grams of the 1 ounce may be marijuana concentrate.

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: No smoking in public places or open spaces
answers.detail: Smoking marijuana in a public place or open space is not allowed and is a petty offense. Consuming it while driving or riding in a vehicle is also not allowed.

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: 2.5 ounces or less, six plants or paraphernalia
answers.detail: Arizona’s courts say Proposition 207 added A.R.S. § 36-2862, which lets some people petition a court for an order sealing their marijuana-related criminal records; the courts’ forms call this expungement. It covers a person arrested, charged, convicted or acquitted, for conduct before November 30, 2020, of possessing, consuming or transporting 2.5 ounces or less of marijuana (no more than 12.5 grams of it concentrate), of possessing, transporting, growing or processing up to six plants at a primary residence for personal use, or of a marijuana paraphernalia offense. Courts have taken petitions since July 12, 2021 and may not charge a filing fee. The petition goes to the court that resolved the case or, if no case was filed, to the Superior Court in the county of the arrest. A prosecuting agency may also file.
answers.citation: A.R.S. § 36-2862, per the Arizona Judicial Branch’s Prop 207 page, petition instructions and court staff presentation

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: Up to 1 ounce or 6 plants, free
answers.detail: An adult may transfer 1 ounce or less, or up to six plants, to another adult 21 or older without payment and without advertising or promoting it.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy cannabis for adult use.
answers.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Every cannabis retailer must hold a Department of Cannabis Control license. The department’s license search finds licensed retailers.
answers.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Having an open container of cannabis while driving or riding in a vehicle is illegal. Cannabis in a vehicle must be in a sealed package or container, or in the trunk. Officers can pull a driver over for a sobriety test if they suspect the driver is under the influence of cannabis.
answers.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: Since January 1, 2024, California employers generally cannot refuse to hire, fire or penalize someone for using cannabis off the job and away from the workplace, or because a drug test finds only non-psychoactive cannabis metabolites. Employers may still act on a scientifically valid test for psychoactive THC, keep a drug-free workplace and bar use, possession or impairment on the job. The protections do not cover employers with four or fewer employees, jobs that need a federal background investigation or security clearance, or employees in the building and construction trades.
answers.citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954, per the Civil Rights Department’s FAQ (January 2024)

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to six cannabis plants at home.
answers.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: People 18 and older with a physician’s recommendation may buy for medicinal use, and medicinal users have higher possession limits.
answers.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 28.5 grams of cannabis and up to 8 grams of concentrated cannabis.
answers.citation: Judicial Council of California, Proposition 64: The Adult Use of Marijuana Act

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: Not in public; private property only
answers.detail: Cannabis may be used on private property, but not in public places such as restaurants or bars.
answers.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: California’s courts say the state reviews records itself: under a 2019 law the Department of Justice identified cases that might qualify under Proposition 64, and a 2023 law required courts to grant relief by March 1, 2023 in cases prosecutors had not challenged. A person can also apply. Someone who has completed a sentence may ask the trial court to dismiss and seal an eligible conviction, or to redesignate it as a misdemeanor or infraction; someone still serving a sentence may petition for resentencing or dismissal.
answers.citation: Cal. Health & Safety Code §§ 11361.8 and 11361.9, per the Judicial Branch of California’s Proposition 64 page

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give away up to 28.5 grams of cannabis and 8 grams of concentrated cannabis to another adult 21 or older without compensation.
answers.citation: Judicial Council of California, Proposition 64: The Adult Use of Marijuana Act

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: It is illegal for anyone under 21 to buy, have or use retail cannabis. Adults 21 and older can have up to 2 ounces.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

answers.question: buying
answers.short: Licensed stores, 1 ounce at a time
answers.detail: Buy retail cannabis only from licensed retail stores, up to 1 ounce at a time, with valid ID showing you are 21 or older.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: A driver affected to the slightest degree can be arrested for DUI or DWAI. A blood test of 5 nanograms or more of active THC per milliliter lets a court assume the driver was under the influence. Neither drivers nor passengers may open cannabis packaging and use the product in a vehicle, even when it is not moving.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Driving and traveling

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Employers may act on a THC drug test
answers.detail: Colorado’s cannabis site says that even though cannabis is legal, employers can still test for THC and make employment decisions based on the results. It advises people to learn their workplace’s policies before using cannabis.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use, “Drug testing at work”

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Each Colorado resident 21 or older may grow up to six plants, with up to three flowering at a time, in an enclosed, locked area that cannot be viewed openly. Local laws can be stricter; Denver caps a home at 12 plants.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Home grow laws

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Colorado’s state site says medical cannabis has its own use and possession rules. DISA’s national map also lists medical use as legal.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use; DISA national map

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older can have up to 2 ounces. Having more can bring charges and fines.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Use is not allowed in public places such as sidewalks, parks and restaurants, or on federal land, including national parks and forests.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Many drug offenses, after a wait
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Colorado’s 2022 Clean Slate law as sealing many drug misdemeanors and felonies after waiting periods, by petition at first and automatically from 2024, with eligibility narrowed by several restrictions. Its table also lists a 2017 law for prior misdemeanor convictions and 2020 pardons for possession of up to two ounces. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give up to 2 ounces to another adult 21 or older but may not sell cannabis, including homegrown cannabis.
answers.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: The state’s adult-use page says residents over 21 can legally possess and consume cannabis, and that possessing 1.5 ounces is legal.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adult-use sales have started at licensed retailers.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Driving under the influence of cannabis is a criminal offense with the same penalties as an alcohol DUI. Connecticut sets no THC blood level; trained officers assess impairment.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Transportation Highway Safety Office, Driving high

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Unless an employer policy bars it
answers.detail: Since July 1, 2022, an employer that is not exempt may not prohibit cannabis use outside work, or act on a positive THC test, unless it has adopted a policy that says otherwise. Exempt employers may regulate off-duty use as they could before the law. Employers generally may not act on cannabis use from before a person applied or was hired. The state’s cannabis site says an employer cannot require a medical marijuana patient to refrain from off-duty use.
answers.citation: State of Connecticut, Adult-Use Cannabis in Connecticut, workplace questions (2021 and 2023)

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to three mature and three immature plants at their primary residence, with a cap of 12 plants per household. Plants must be indoors, not visible from the street and out of reach of anyone under 21.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Can I grow cannabis at home?

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Connecticut’s medical marijuana program continues to serve patients alongside adult use.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: The state’s adult-use page says possessing 1.5 ounces of cannabis is legal.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: Local rules; banned in state parks
answers.detail: You generally cannot smoke or vape cannabis anywhere tobacco smoking or vaping is banned. Cities and towns may regulate public consumption, and use is prohibited in state parks, on state beaches and on state waters.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Where can I use cannabis?

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Some possession convictions; others by petition
answers.detail: Connecticut’s Clean Slate site says convictions under General Statutes § 21a-279(c) imposed from January 1, 2000 through September 30, 2015 were set to be erased automatically on January 1, 2023, with nothing for the person to do. Others need a petition to the court, accepted since July 1, 2022: possession of four ounces or less under § 21a-279 imposed before January 1, 2000 or from October 1, 2015 through June 30, 2021; cannabis paraphernalia under § 21a-267(a) imposed before July 1, 2021; and making, selling or giving four ounces or less, or six plants grown at home for personal use, under § 21a-277(b) imposed before July 1, 2021. There is no official petition form; the court either erases the conviction without a hearing or schedules one.
answers.citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 54-142d and 54-142v, per the State of Connecticut’s Clean Slate pages on cannabis erasure

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: Free gifts in a bona fide social relationship
answers.detail: People with a bona fide social relationship may give each other cannabis without payment or exchange and not tied to a sale. Gifts tied to donations, paid-entry locations or event giveaways are prohibited, and medical marijuana may not be gifted.
answers.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Can I gift cannabis to other individuals?

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: A person at least 21 may possess 2 ounces or less and use marijuana on private property.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: DC police guidance says selling any amount of marijuana to another person is illegal. Licensed medical cannabis retailers serve registered patients.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department; DC Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Operating a vehicle or boat under the influence of marijuana is an arrestable offense, and consuming marijuana in a vehicle in public space is a violation.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: An employer may not refuse to hire, fire, suspend, demote, fail to promote or penalize someone for using cannabis, for being a medical cannabis patient, or for cannabinoid metabolites in a drug test without other signs of impairment. Employers may act when the job is designated safety-sensitive, when federal law, a federal contract or funding requires it, when cannabis is used or possessed at work, or when the employee is impaired at work. They may still test after an accident or on reasonable suspicion. The act took effect on October 22, 2022; its protections applied no earlier than 365 days after the Mayor approved it.
answers.citation: D.C. Law 24-190, Cannabis Employment Protections Amendment Act of 2022, section 102

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: An adult may cultivate up to six plants within their residence, no more than three of them mature.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

answers.question: medical

answers.citation: DC Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: A person at least 21 may possess 2 ounces or less.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Use is prohibited on any street, sidewalk, alley, park or parking area. Using medical marijuana in public is also a criminal offense.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists the District as letting people with records for conduct that was later legalized or decriminalized file to have them sealed. Not yet checked against the District’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: An adult may transfer 1 ounce or less to another person 21 or older when no payment or exchange of goods or services is involved.
answers.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

answers.question: adult-use

answers.question: buying

answers.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, sales launch announcement (August 1, 2025)

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: The Office of the Marijuana Commissioner says driving under the influence is still illegal.
answers.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Delaware as barring employers from discriminating against a cardholder for that status or for a positive marijuana test, unless the person used, possessed or was impaired by marijuana at work. Its chart lists an exception where the employer would lose a federal monetary or licensing benefit. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: 16 Del. C. § 4905A, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Home cultivation remains prohibited.

answers.question: medical

answers.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner

answers.question: possession

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Public consumption remains prohibited.
answers.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

Its table says the work has been slow because records are not digitized. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing

answers.detail: Adults may share marijuana with other adults as long as no money is exchanged.
answers.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Florida has no adult-use law. Possessing 20 grams of cannabis or less is a first-degree misdemeanor; larger amounts are felonies.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Medical marijuana and low-THC cannabis are available to qualified patients. A qualified physician orders them, and licensed medical marijuana treatment centers are the only businesses allowed to dispense them.
answers.citation: Florida Office of Medical Marijuana Use

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Georgia has no adult-use law. The state’s Access to Medical Cannabis Commission says adult-use marijuana is not legal and that growing, possessing and smoking marijuana are crimes. Possessing 1 ounce or less is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 12 months in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.
answers.citation: Georgia Access to Medical Cannabis Commission FAQ; O.C.G.A. 16-13-2(b)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Georgia’s commission runs a medical cannabis registry and licenses dispensaries. DISA’s national map lists Georgia as CBD oil only.
answers.citation: Georgia Access to Medical Cannabis Commission; DISA national map

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Hawaii has no adult-use law. Possessing 3 grams of marijuana or less is a violation with a $130 fine rather than a crime, and distribution remains illegal. That is how the Attorney General’s office described current law in February 2024; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Haw. Rev. Stat. 712-1249(2), per Department of the Attorney General testimony (2024); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Patients must register with the Department of Health before medical use. The department also runs a dispensary program that serves qualified patients.
answers.citation: Hawaii Department of Health, Medical cannabis

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Iowa has no adult-use law. A first conviction for possessing marijuana can bring up to six months in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. Penalties rise for repeat offenses.
answers.citation: Iowa Code 124.401(5)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services registers patients 18 and older who have a health care practitioner’s certification, with cards good for one year. Cardholders buy from five licensed dispensaries. The program page also links a waiver form for the limit of 4.5 grams of THC per 90 days.
answers.citation: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Medical cannabis patients and caregivers

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Idaho has no adult-use law. Possessing 3 ounces of marijuana or less is a misdemeanor, with a fine of at least $300 for anyone 18 or older. More than 3 ounces is a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000, or both.
answers.citation: Idaho Code 37-2732(e)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Idaho has no medical marijuana law. The possession penalties in Idaho Code 37-2732 make no exception for medical use.
answers.citation: Idaho Code 37-2732

answers.question: adult-use

answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: 291 dispensaries were licensed to sell cannabis to adults 21 and older as of November 1, 2026.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer

answers.question: driving
answers.short: Illegal at 5 ng/ml THC in blood
answers.detail: Driving is prohibited with 5 nanograms of THC per milliliter of whole blood, or 10 nanograms in another bodily substance, within two hours of driving.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Illinois as giving limited protection: employers may not penalize someone solely for being a registered patient or caregiver, but may enforce drug-testing, zero-tolerance and drug-free workplace policies that are applied without discrimination. Its chart lists an exception for federal law or loss of a federal benefit. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: 410 ILCS 130/40 and 130/50, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: Registered patients only, up to 5 plants
answers.detail: Only registered qualifying medical cannabis patients may grow, up to five plants at home.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Illinois registers medical cannabis patients and caregivers. 191 dispensaries were licensed to sell medical cannabis as of November 1, 2026.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Residents over 21: 60 grams of flower, 1,000 milligrams of THC in infused products and 10 grams of concentrate. Non-residents: 30 grams, 500 milligrams and 5 grams. The amounts are cumulative.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: The law does not permit using cannabis in any public place, and cannabis cannot be used in a motor vehicle.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Under 30 grams: automatic if no conviction
answers.detail: Illinois’s cannabis site says minor cannabis offenses that did not end in a conviction, usually possession, manufacture, delivery or intent to deliver under 30 grams, are expunged automatically and removed from the public record. Minor offenses that ended in a conviction may be pardoned by the Governor, which expunges the record, and county State’s Attorneys may ask courts to vacate and expunge convictions. The site names New Leaf Illinois, a statewide, state-funded initiative, for free legal help.
answers.citation: Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, per the State of Illinois cannabis site’s Expungement page

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give cannabis as a purely non-commercial gift to another adult 21 or older. Medical cannabis patients may not gift their medical cannabis.
answers.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Indiana has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor. It is a Class A misdemeanor with a prior drug conviction, and a Level 6 felony with a prior drug conviction and 30 grams or more.
answers.citation: Indiana Code 35-48-4-11

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Indiana has no medical marijuana law. Its possession statute, Indiana Code 35-48-4-11, makes no exception for medical use.
answers.citation: Indiana Code 35-48-4-11

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Kansas has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a Class B nonperson misdemeanor. One prior conviction makes it a Class A misdemeanor, and two or more make it a drug felony.

answers.question: medical
answers.short: Legal defense for CBD treatment oil
answers.detail: Kansas law gives an affirmative defense to a person charged with possessing a cannabidiol treatment preparation for a debilitating medical condition who has a letter from a Kansas physician dated within the past 15 months. It is a defense in court, not a program for buying medical marijuana.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Kentucky has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor with no more than 45 days in jail. The offense does not apply to medical cannabis cardholders.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Senate Bill 47 legalized medical cannabis effective January 1, 2025. The Office of Medical Cannabis runs the program.
answers.citation: Kentucky Office of Medical Cannabis

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Louisiana has no adult-use law. Without medical authorization, possessing 14 grams or less brings a summons and a fine of up to $100. A first conviction for more than 14 grams can bring up to six months in jail, a $500 fine, or both.

answers.question: employment
answers.short: State employees who are medical patients
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Louisiana as protecting state government employees only: a state employer may not penalize an employee solely for a positive marijuana test if the employee has a physician’s recommendation. Its chart lists exceptions for use or impairment at work and for safety and law-enforcement roles. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: La. R.S. 49:1016, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Louisiana Department of Health regulates medical marijuana. A patient with a recommendation from an authorized clinician buys from licensed retailers, and raw flower is limited to 71 grams (2.5 ounces) every 14 days. State law exempts patients in the program from the possession penalties.
answers.citation: Louisiana Department of Health; La. R.S. 40:966(F)

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: You must be 21 or older to buy or grow adult-use marijuana. Adults may carry up to 2 ounces and keep up to 10 ounces at home.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Licensed marijuana establishments sell to adults. Visitors from other states must be 21 or older and show a valid government-issued ID.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: It is illegal to drive under the influence of cannabis or to have an open container of marijuana in the passenger area of a car.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Medical patients, under a court ruling
answers.detail: The Cannabis Control Commission tells people to check the rules where they work: employers may have their own policies on marijuana use. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists a protection for medical patients through a court ruling: the state’s high court held that the anti-discrimination law covers disabled employees who use medical cannabis, so an employer must consider a reasonable accommodation unless it would be an undue hardship (Barbuto v. Advantage Sales and Marketing); that part is not yet checked against an official source.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws; Barbuto v. Advantage Sales and Marketing and G.L. c. 151B, § 4, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults may grow up to six plants for personal use, and up to 12 plants when two or more adults live in the home.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Medical Use of Marijuana Program serves registered patients and caregivers. Out-of-state residents cannot buy medical marijuana in Massachusetts.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults may carry up to 2 ounces and possess up to 10 ounces at home.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Cannabis cannot be used in any form in public places or on federal land.
answers.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Amounts that have since been decriminalized
answers.detail: Massachusetts’s courts say a person can ask a judge to expunge, meaning permanently destroy, the court records of marijuana offenses where the amount involved has since been decriminalized (G.L. c. 276, § 100K¼, in effect since November 9, 2022). The petitioner must show the amount was two ounces or less, ten ounces or less inside a primary residence, or six or fewer plants for personal use or twelve or fewer on the premises. The petition is filed with the clerk of the court that heard the case, with a copy to the District Attorney, and the court is to act within 30 days. Separately, the Governor’s pardon forgives state convictions for simple possession before March 13, 2024; the courts’ law library says most people need not act and may request a pardon certificate.
answers.citation: G.L. c. 276, § 100K¼, per the Massachusetts Trial Court’s petition form (11/22) and the Trial Court Law Libraries’ criminal records page

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give away up to 2 ounces of marijuana, or the equivalent in products set by the Cannabis Control Commission, to another adult 21 or older without payment, as long as it is not advertised or promoted. The 2-ounce limit took effect April 19, 2026.
answers.citation: M.G.L. c. 94G, § 7(a)(4), as amended by Acts 2026, c. 65

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration states that cannabis is legal for adults 21 and older.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, BeCannabisSmart

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy from a licensed dispensary after showing government-issued photo ID, up to the personal use amount.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: It is illegal to smoke or use cannabis while driving. Driving while impaired by cannabis carries the same penalties as driving drunk.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, BeCannabisSmart guide (October 2025)

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Fire and rescue workers who are patients
answers.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration says the Cannabis Reform Act does not address cannabis use or impairment in the workplace, or employer drug screening: people remain subject to existing laws and to workplace policies, including policies that ban cannabis use. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists one protection, for fire and rescue employees who are certified medical cannabis patients (Md. Code, State Gov’t § 20-606); that part is not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs; Md. Code, State Gov’t § 20-606, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to two plants at home, out of public view. A household may have no more than two, however many adults live there.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration runs a medical cannabis program alongside adult use.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 1.5 oz flower, 12 g concentrate, 750 mg THC
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 1.5 ounces of flower, 12 grams of concentrated cannabis, or products with up to 750 milligrams of THC. This is the personal use amount.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Smoking cannabis is prohibited in all indoor and outdoor public spaces, including parks, event venues, bars, restaurants, streets and sidewalks.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, BeCannabisSmart guide (October 2025)

answers.question: record-relief

answers.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration says the 2022 and 2023 laws set up a process to expunge cases in which possession of less than 10 grams of cannabis is the only charge, and include other expungement provisions. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists that expungement as automatic and due by July 2024, says the state appears to have missed the deadline, and notes that the governor’s June 2024 pardons do not themselves expunge a record; those points are not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs; Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may share up to the personal use amount with each other without payment. Gifts tied to another transaction, or offered with a sale of goods or services, do not count.
answers.citation: Maryland Department of Legislative Services, HB 441 fiscal and policy note (2024), current law

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Maine’s adult use program serves consumers 21 and older, who may possess up to 2.5 ounces.
answers.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy up to 2.5 ounces from a licensed cannabis store, no more than 10 grams of it concentrate.

answers.question: driving
answers.short: OUI applies; no use in vehicles
answers.detail: Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal and can bring an OUI charge. The driver and passengers may not consume cannabis in a vehicle on a public way.
answers.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions; 28-B M.R.S. § 1501(2)(B)

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Maine as barring an employer from refusing to employ or otherwise penalizing a person solely for being a qualifying patient or caregiver, unless that would violate federal law or cost a federal contract or funding. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: 22 M.R.S. § 2430-C(3), per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Each resident 21 or older may grow up to six mature plants, 12 immature plants and an unlimited number of seedlings.
answers.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Maine runs both a medical cannabis program and an adult use program.
answers.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 2.5 ounces, of which up to 10 grams may be concentrate.
answers.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Use in any form is prohibited in public places. Neither the driver nor passengers may consume cannabis in a vehicle on a public way.
answers.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Maine as allowing petition-based sealing for some cannabis offenses under a 2024 law (LD 2236). Its table says the sealing is not comprehensive and that some professional licensing bodies can still see the records. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may transfer up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 10 grams of it concentrate, to another adult 21 or older without remuneration. Remuneration includes a donation or other payment received as part of the transfer.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Michigan law allows personal possession and use of marijuana by people 21 and older.
answers.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Consumer connection

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Licensed marijuana retailers may sell to adults 21 and older. Adults may purchase and possess up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate.

answers.question: driving
