answers.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Employers may enforce workplace drug policies
answers.detail: Michigan’s adult-use law says it does not require an employer to permit or accommodate conduct the act allows in any workplace or on the employer’s property. It does not prevent an employer from refusing to hire, discharging or disciplining a person for violating a workplace drug policy or for working while under the influence of marihuana.

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults may grow up to 12 plants for personal use within their residence, with no more than 12 plants on the premises at once.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Michigan Medical Marijuana Program registers patients and caregivers.
answers.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Consumer connection

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 2.5 oz (15 g concentrate); 10 oz at home
answers.detail: Adults may possess up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate. Within their residence they may keep up to 10 ounces, plus marijuana from plants grown there.

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: The adult-use law does not authorize consuming marijuana in public.
answers.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Clean Slate after 7 years; marijuana by application
answers.detail: Michigan’s Attorney General says the State Police run a daily automatic process under the Clean Slate laws, which cover criminal records in general and are not specific to cannabis: misdemeanors can be set aside after seven years (any number punishable by less than 93 days, up to four of 93 days or more) and up to two felonies after ten years, with no application. Separately, under MCL 780.621e a person convicted of a misdemeanor marijuana offense (possession, use, selling paraphernalia or a matching local ordinance) may apply to the convicting court on form MC 227a; the conduct is presumed to be something that would not have been a crime on or after December 6, 2018, and if the prosecutor does not answer within 60 days the court must set the conviction aside. A set-aside removes the conviction from public view; law enforcement and some licensing agencies may still see it.
answers.citation: MCL 780.621e and 780.621g, per the State Court Administrative Office’s Clean Slate overview and the Department of Attorney General’s Expungement Assistance page

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give away up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate, to another adult 21 or older without payment, as long as the transfer is not advertised or promoted.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: A person 21 or older may possess up to 2 ounces of flower in public and 2 pounds at home, plus 8 grams of concentrate and edibles with up to 800 milligrams of THC in total.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adult-use cannabis is available for purchase at any licensed adult-use retailer.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Guide to Safer Cannabis Use (June 2026)

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal and subject to additional DWI sanctions.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: An employer may not refuse to hire an applicant, or discipline or discharge an employee, for using lawful consumable products off the employer’s premises during nonworking hours. Cannabis flower, cannabis products and lower-potency hemp edibles count as lawful products under Minnesota law. Employers may still act on use, possession or impairment during working hours, on work premises or while operating the employer’s vehicle or equipment, or where federal or state law requires it or a federal benefit would be lost. Exceptions include bona fide occupational requirements and conflicts of interest.
answers.citation: Minn. Stat. § 181.938

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: Up to 8 plants per home, 4 mature
answers.detail: Plants must be kept in an enclosed, locked space that is not open to public view.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Office of Cannabis Management runs Minnesota’s medical cannabis program.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 2 ounces in public, 2 pounds at home
answers.detail: Also 8 grams of concentrate and edibles infused with a combined 800 milligrams of THC or less.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Use and possession are banned at public and charter schools, state correctional facilities, federal property, federally subsidized housing and an employer’s premises, and while driving or operating heavy machinery.
answers.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Certain misdemeanors; a board reviews felonies
answers.detail: Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension says the Adult-Use Cannabis Act requires automatic expungement of certain earlier cannabis records; it expunged the qualifying records in its system in May 2024 and will review again in 2026. The state’s cannabis record site says these are misdemeanor convictions and certain offenses that did not end in a conviction, that sealed records will not show on most background checks, and that no one is notified: a person can check the courts’ online case search or a courthouse terminal. Felony and gross misdemeanor records go to the Cannabis Expungement Board for review; no application is needed, though a person may apply for earlier consideration. The separate Clean Slate Act, in effect since January 1, 2025, automatically seals certain other records.
answers.citation: Minn. Stat. §§ 609A.055 and 609A.06, per the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension’s Expungements page and the state’s cannabis record FAQs

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: 2 oz flower, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg, free
answers.detail: Adults may give, for no remuneration, up to 2 ounces of flower, 8 grams of concentrate, or an edible with up to 800 milligrams of THC to another adult 21 or older.
answers.citation: Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(6)

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Consumers at least 21 years old may possess up to 3 ounces of marijuana.
answers.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Consumers must show a valid government-issued photo ID to buy adult-use products at a dispensary.
answers.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: The adult-use section of the constitution does not allow operating a vehicle under the influence of marijuana, consuming it while operating one, or smoking it in a vehicle that is being operated. A conviction requires evidence that the driver was in fact under the influence, not just THC or its metabolites in the system.
answers.citation: Missouri Constitution, Article XIV, Section 2

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services says Article XIV of the state constitution, sections 1 and 2, provides certain employment-related protections for patients and consumers, and that employment questions are outside its authority. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists the patient protections as covering lawful use off the premises in nonworking hours and positive drug tests, with exceptions for impairment at work, loss of a federal benefit and jobs where use affects performance or safety; that part, and what the constitution gives adult consumers, is not yet checked against the state’s own text.
answers.citation: Mo. Const. art. XIV, §§ 1 and 2, per the Department of Health and Senior Services’ FAQ; Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: With a state card; 6 flowering plants
answers.detail: Consumers need a personal cultivation identification card, valid for 12 months and renewable. A cardholder may grow six flowering plants, six nonflowering plants over 14 inches and six under 14 inches, 18 in all. Flowering plants must be labeled with the consumer’s name. The plants, and any harvest beyond 3 ounces, must be kept in an enclosed, locked facility at a private residence.
answers.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs; Cannabis cultivation fact sheet

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Missouri issues medical marijuana ID cards to patients.
answers.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Cannabis regulation

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Consumers may possess up to 3 ounces at any time.
answers.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: The constitution does not allow consuming marijuana in a public place outside a licensed area, or smoking it where tobacco smoking is prohibited.
answers.citation: Missouri Constitution, Article XIV, Section 2

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Offenses that are no longer crimes
answers.detail: Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services says the law lets people with certain non-violent marijuana offenses petition for release from incarceration, parole or probation and to have their records expunged, and that sales-tax revenue pays the government bodies that carry out expungement of certain marijuana offenses. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Amendment 3 as directing courts to expunge offenses that are no longer crimes without a petition, misdemeanors by June 8, 2023 and felonies by December 8, 2023; that part is not yet checked against the state’s own text.
answers.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs; Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may deliver or distribute up to 3 ounces of dried, unprocessed marijuana, or its equivalent, without consideration. Giving marijuana to anyone under 21 is not allowed.
answers.citation: Missouri Constitution, Article XIV, Section 2

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Mississippi has no adult-use law. The state Health Department’s medical cannabis program says recreational use and possession remain illegal. Its patient toolkit lists a $250 fine for a first offense of up to 30 grams outside the program, jail time for repeat offenses, and a felony for more than 30 grams.
answers.citation: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program toolkit: patient rights and applicable laws (2026)

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Employers need not permit medical cannabis use
answers.detail: Mississippi’s Medical Cannabis Program says the law does not require employers to permit medical cannabis use or to exempt employees from drug testing.
answers.citation: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program, Patient Rights & Applicable Laws (program toolkit)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program accepts applications from patients, caregivers, medical practitioners, facilities and services.
answers.citation: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older with ID may buy from licensed dispensaries in counties where adult sales are allowed (green counties). Possession limits are 1 ounce of flower, 8 grams of concentrate and 800 milligrams of THC in products. Using marijuana in a public place is prohibited.
answers.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older with ID may buy from licensed dispensaries in counties where adult sales are allowed (green counties).
answers.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: State law does not permit operating a vehicle under the influence of marijuana, consuming it while operating a vehicle, or smoking or consuming it in the passenger seat of an enclosed vehicle while it is being operated.

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: Marijuana is a lawful product under Montana’s lawful-product law. An employer may not refuse to employ someone, or discriminate in pay, promotion or other terms of employment, because the person legally uses a lawful product off the employer’s premises during nonworking hours. The rule does not apply to use that affects job performance or the safety of other employees, or that conflicts with a bona fide occupational qualification. An employer also does not violate it by acting in the belief that an established substance abuse or alcohol policy, a professional contract or a collective bargaining agreement permits the action.

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to two mature plants and two seedlings at a private residence, and no more than twice that at one residence. Plants, and any harvest over 1 ounce, must be kept in a locked space out of public view, and a grower who does not own the home needs the owner’s written permission. The Department of Revenue describes home growing as open to Montana residents.
answers.citation: MCA 16-12-106(1)(c); Montana Department of Revenue, Know before you grow

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Montana residents with a Montana physician’s recommendation can get a one-year registry card for $20 and buy up to 1 ounce a day and 5 ounces a month at any licensed dispensary.
answers.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, cardholder information

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 1 oz flower, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg THC
answers.detail: Possession limits are 1 ounce of flower, 8 grams of concentrate and 800 milligrams of THC in products.
answers.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: State law does not permit consuming marijuana in a public place, except as allowed by the department, or on public transportation. Smoking it in a public place can bring a civil fine of up to $50.
answers.citation: MCA 16-12-108(1)(k) and 16-12-106(4); Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Acts the marijuana law now permits
answers.detail: A person who has completed a sentence for an act that Montana’s marijuana law now permits, or punishes less severely, may petition the sentencing court to expunge the conviction or to redesignate it as a misdemeanor or civil infraction. The court presumes the person qualifies unless the county attorney gives a reasonable basis otherwise, and no hearing is needed unless the person asks for one. A person still serving a sentence may petition for expungement or resentencing. Filing does not affect a person’s separate right to petition for misdemeanor expungement.

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may transfer up to 1 ounce of usable marijuana to another adult 21 or older, or to a registered cardholder, without consideration. No more than 8 grams may be concentrate and no more than 800 milligrams of THC may be in solid edibles.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: North Carolina has no adult-use law. Possessing half an ounce or less is a Class 3 misdemeanor. More than half an ounce, up to 1.5 ounces, is a Class 1 misdemeanor, and more than 1.5 ounces is a Class I felony.
answers.citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. 90-95(d)(4)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: State law lets a caregiver possess and give hemp extract with less than 0.9% THC and at least 5% CBD to a person with intractable epilepsy, with a certificate of analysis for the extract.
answers.citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. 90-94.1

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: North Dakota has no adult-use law. Without a medical card, possessing less than half an ounce is an infraction. Half an ounce up to 500 grams is a class B misdemeanor, and more than 500 grams is a class A misdemeanor.

answers.question: medical
answers.short: Yes, with a state registry card
answers.detail: North Dakota residents with written certification from a North Dakota-licensed provider can apply for a registry card ($40). Cardholders may buy only from the state’s eight registered dispensaries; state law does not protect marijuana bought anywhere else.
answers.citation: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, Medical Marijuana Patients

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Nebraska has no adult-use law. Without a medical recommendation, a first offense for 1 ounce or less is an infraction with a citation and a $300 fine, and a drug education course may be required. More than 1 ounce, up to 1 pound, is a Class III misdemeanor.
answers.citation: Neb. Rev. Stat. 28-416

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Voters approved Initiative 437 in 2024. It lets a qualified patient with a health care practitioner’s written recommendation use and possess up to 5 ounces of cannabis. The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission regulates the program; its application page says only cultivator and manufacturer license applications have opened so far.
answers.citation: Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-24,104; Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: New Hampshire has no adult-use law. Since 2017, possessing three-quarters of an ounce of marijuana or less has been a violation, not a crime, for people 18 and older; possessing more is a misdemeanor. That is how the Attorney General’s office described the law in a 2019 court brief; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: RSA 318-B:2-c and 318-B:26, II(c), per the State’s brief in case No. 2018-0647 (2019); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Medical patients, under a court ruling
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists New Hampshire as protecting medical patients through a court ruling, not the therapeutic cannabis law: the state Supreme Court held in 2022 that therapeutic cannabis use may call for a reasonable accommodation under the Law Against Discrimination. Its chart notes the therapeutic cannabis law does not require accommodating use on an employer’s premises. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Paine v. Ride-Away (N.H. 2022); RSA 354-A; RSA 126-X:3, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Therapeutic Cannabis Program issues registry ID cards that let cardholders buy from Alternative Treatment Centers.
answers.citation: New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, Therapeutic Cannabis Program

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may have up to 6 ounces of cannabis.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Buy at the New Jersey licensed dispensaries listed in the state’s dispensary finder.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: The state’s impaired-driving laws apply to driving under the influence of cannabis.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Cannabis use alone cannot decide hiring or firing
answers.detail: The Cannabis Regulatory Commission says general cannabis use cannot be a determining factor in hiring or firing someone, and that an employer may not take adverse action solely because a drug test finds cannabinoid metabolites from lawful use. Employers may keep a drug- and alcohol-free workplace and may require a drug test on reasonable suspicion of use at work, on signs of impairment, in a random testing program or after a workplace accident. A positive test together with documented signs of impairment during work hours may support action. Employers bound by a federal contract may follow federal rules.
answers.citation: N.J.S.A. 24:6I-52, per the Cannabis Regulatory Commission’s workplace page and guidance (September 9, 2022)

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: New Jersey law does not allow personal growing.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Legal cannabis in New Jersey (September 2025)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: New Jersey runs a Medicinal Cannabis Program for patients.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may have up to 6 ounces.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Cannabis smoking is allowed where cigarette smoking is permitted unless stated otherwise, and landlords may prohibit use. Licensed consumption areas admit only people 21 and older with photo ID.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The New Jersey Judiciary says it expunges eligible marijuana and hashish cases automatically, with no request needed, under the Marijuana Decriminalization Law; by February 2022 it had cleared more than 362,000 cases. An expunged case leaves the public court record and need not be reported on applications for jobs, housing or college. A person who believes a case should have qualified can file a motion for judicial review, and can get a certification of expungement from the court that heard the case or the Superior Court Clerk’s Office in Trenton.
answers.citation: New Jersey Judiciary, Marijuana Record Expungement (February 1, 2022)

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give up to 28.35 grams (1 ounce) to another adult 21 or older and may not accept any payment or compensation for it.
answers.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may cultivate, buy, possess and consume cannabis.
answers.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis in New Mexico

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: The first licensed adult-use sales began on April 1, 2022.
answers.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis in New Mexico

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: The state’s cannabis FAQ says using cannabis or cannabis products while driving is illegal.
answers.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis FAQs

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists New Mexico as barring employers from taking adverse action against an applicant or employee for conduct its medical cannabis law allows. Its chart lists exceptions for federal law or loss of a federal benefit, and for jobs the employer deems safety-sensitive. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: N.M. Stat. § 26-2B-9, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: 12 plants per adult, 6 mature; 12 mature per home
answers.detail: An adult 21 or older may grow up to 12 plants at a private residence, no more than six of them mature. A household with several adults may have no more than 12 mature plants.
answers.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Personal use of cannabis

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Department of Health continues to oversee the medical cannabis patient program.
answers.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis in New Mexico

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 2 oz, 16 g extract, 800 mg edibles in public
answers.detail: Outside their home, adults may have up to 2 ounces of cannabis, 16 grams of extract and 800 milligrams of edibles. More may be kept at home if it is not visible from a public place.

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: No; private homes or licensed lounges
answers.detail: Consumption must take place at a private residence or a licensed consumption lounge. Using cannabis in public spaces such as restaurants, parks and sidewalks can bring a fine of up to $50.
answers.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis FAQs

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: New Mexico’s Regulation and Licensing Department says the Criminal Records Expungement Act, in effect since January 1, 2020, lets a qualifying person petition a court to expunge certain criminal records, including marijuana-related records, and points to the state courts’ expungement page. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists a separate law that reviews and expunges convictions for legalized conduct automatically, limited since 2023 to cannabis convictions that stand alone; that part is not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: NMSA 1978, §§ 29-3A-1 to 29-3A-9, per the Regulation and Licensing Department’s FAQs; Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may transfer cannabis to another adult 21 or older without financial consideration, up to the amount lawfully purchased and obtained under state law.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older can legally possess up to 2.5 ounces of cannabis and up to 1/4 ounce of concentrate.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adults may buy cannabis only from state-licensed retail stores and must show ID proving they are 21 or older.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: It is illegal to drive under the influence of cannabis.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: It is unlawful for a Nevada employer to refuse to hire a prospective employee because a screening test shows marijuana. That does not cover applicants to be firefighters or emergency medical technicians, jobs that require driving and for which law requires screening tests, or jobs the employer determines could adversely affect the safety of others. It gives way to an employment contract or collective bargaining agreement and to federal law, and does not cover positions funded by a federal grant. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists no protection for current employees’ adult use, and lists a duty to try to reasonably accommodate medical cardholders’ use away from work (NRS 678C.850); those two points are not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: NRS 613.132; Marijuana Policy Project’s table and chart for the other points

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: Only if no store within 25 miles
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to six plants each and 12 per household, but only if no state-licensed retail cannabis store is within 25 miles of the home.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Cannabis Compliance Board oversees medical cannabis, including patient ID cards.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older can legally possess up to 2.5 ounces of cannabis and up to 1/4 ounce of concentrated cannabis.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Cannabis cannot be used in any public place, or in a moving vehicle even as a passenger.
answers.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Nevada as allowing people, under a 2019 law, to have past convictions sealed when the conduct, such as marijuana possession, has been legalized or decriminalized. Its table also lists a 2020 pardons-board resolution for possession of one ounce or less from 1986 to 2017. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: Up to 2.5 oz or 1/4 oz concentrate, free
answers.detail: An adult may deliver up to 2.5 ounces of usable cannabis or 1/4 ounce of concentrated cannabis to another adult 21 or older without remuneration, if the delivery is not advertised or promoted.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess, buy and transport up to 3 ounces of cannabis and 24 grams of concentrate. Up to 5 pounds may be kept at home if secured from anyone under 21.
answers.citation: N.Y. Penal Law §§ 222.05 and 222.15; Office of Cannabis Management

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy up to 3 ounces of cannabis and 24 grams of concentrate.
answers.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.05; Office of Cannabis Management

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Driving impaired by a drug is treated like alcohol-impaired driving. Cannabis in a vehicle must be in a closed container, and smoking cannabis in a vehicle is illegal for drivers and passengers.
answers.citation: N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1192; Office of Cannabis Management

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: Employers generally may not act against workers for lawful off-duty cannabis use away from the workplace and without employer property. Employers may still act when required by state or federal law, when a worker shows specific articulable signs of impairment on the job, or when allowing it would violate federal law or risk a federal contract or funding.
answers.citation: N.Y. Labor Law § 201-d

answers.question: home-grow
answers.short: 3 mature and 3 immature plants per adult
answers.detail: No more than six mature and six immature plants per residence, only at a private residence and secured from anyone under 21. Localities may regulate but not effectively ban home growing.
answers.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.15; Office of Cannabis Management, Home cultivation FAQs

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: A certifying provider may certify a patient for any condition they judge suitable. Patients or caregivers may buy up to a 60-day supply. A 2025 law (S3294A) lets registered patients and caregivers 18 and older grow at home and lets patients certified in other states buy in New York.
answers.citation: Office of Cannabis Management, Patients; Senate Bill S3294A (2025)

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 3 ounces and 24 g concentrate; 5 pounds at home
answers.detail: Up to 5 pounds may be kept at home if secured from anyone under 21.
answers.citation: N.Y. Penal Law §§ 222.05 and 222.15

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: Where tobacco smoking is allowed, with exceptions
answers.detail: Not in a motor vehicle, where smoking or vaping is banned, on school grounds or buses, or on federal property. Breaking these limits carries a civil penalty of up to $25 or up to 20 hours of community service.
answers.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.10; Office of Cannabis Management

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: Convictions under the listed marijuana offenses (possession up to 16 ounces or sale up to 25 grams) are expunged automatically, with no motion or fee and no notice sent. Expunged cases do not appear on background checks and need not be disclosed. Other marijuana convictions require a CPL 440.46-a motion. Separately, the Clean Slate Act, in effect since November 16, 2024, provides automatic sealing of eligible convictions for certain civil background checks; courts have until November 16, 2027 to finish setting it up. Sex crimes and non-drug Class A felonies are not eligible.
answers.citation: N.Y. Unified Court System: cannabis expungement page and Clean Slate Act page

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give up to 3 ounces and 24 grams of concentrate to another adult 21 or older without compensation. “Gifting” tied to a sale is not lawful sharing.
answers.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.05

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may use and possess marijuana bought from a licensed Ohio dispensary, up to 2.5 ounces of plant material and 15 grams of extract in total, counting homegrown marijuana.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Adult-use marijuana must be bought from a licensed Ohio dispensary.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Neither the adult-use nor the medical law allows driving under the influence. Driving with marijuana or its metabolite at or above set blood or urine concentrations is an offense even without shown impairment, and medical registration is not a defense.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221 and 4511.19

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Employers may act on marijuana use
answers.detail: Ohio’s marijuana law does not require employers to allow or accommodate marijuana use, possession or distribution. Employers may refuse to hire, discharge or discipline someone because of marijuana use, and may keep drug-testing, drug-free workplace and zero-tolerance policies. This applies to medical and adult-use marijuana alike.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.28

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Subject to secured-area, primary-residence and other statutory conditions.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.04

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: A patient registered with the Division of Cannabis Control, with a certified physician’s recommendation for a qualifying condition, may possess up to a 90-day supply bought from a licensed dispensary. Caregivers register separately.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.22 and 3796.08

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: The limit counts dispensary and homegrown marijuana together.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Using adult-use or homegrown marijuana in a public place is prohibited. Use is legal at a private residence, subject to the property owner’s rules.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.04

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: An application-based process to expunge specified marijuana and hashish possession cases from before March 20, 2026. Eligibility and court procedures are stated in the statute.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 2953.321

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: Same amounts, free, on private property only
answers.detail: An adult may give the same amounts to another adult in a single day, without payment, only on private residential or agricultural property. Other transfers require a license.
answers.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Oklahoma has no adult-use law. In March 2023, more than 61% of voters rejected State Question 820, which would have legalized recreational marijuana. National compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Oklahoma State Senate (2023); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Oklahoma as barring employers from penalizing an applicant or employee solely for being a medical marijuana licensee or for a positive marijuana test. Its chart lists exceptions for federal law or funding, no valid license, use or impairment at work and safety-sensitive jobs. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: 63 O.S. § 427.8, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority regulates the state’s medical marijuana program.
answers.citation: Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older can possess and use cannabis within set limits.
answers.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Marijuana items may be bought at an OLCC-licensed retail location. A customer may buy up to 2 ounces of usable marijuana at one time or in one day.
answers.citation: Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Driving while impaired, including by cannabis, remains illegal.
answers.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission says the state’s cannabis law does not change existing employment law. Employers who test for drugs may keep doing so, and whether a person can be fired for using marijuana depends on the employer’s policies.
answers.citation: Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: The personal possession limits include four marijuana plants.
answers.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Oregon Medical Marijuana Act allows medical use for qualifying medical conditions.
answers.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Also 16 ounces of solid products or concentrates, 72 ounces of liquid products and 1 ounce of extracts bought from a marijuana retailer.
answers.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Public use remains illegal.
answers.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

answers.question: record-relief
answers.short: Qualifying convictions, no fee or waiting period
answers.detail: Oregon’s courts say ORS 475C.397 requires a court to set aside a qualifying marijuana conviction, with no waiting period and no filing fee, unless the prosecutor objects within 30 days that the conviction does not qualify. On the statewide form a person declares that the conduct took place before July 1, 2015 and that the conviction was for conduct described in ORS 475C.305 or for possessing less than one ounce of dried marijuana. The same form asks the court under ORS 137.222 to lower a conviction for an offense that has since been reduced. A set-aside seals the record and the person is treated as not previously convicted. Separately, on November 21, 2022 the Governor pardoned state-court convictions for possessing one ounce or less in pre-2015 cases where the person was 21 or older, it was the only charge and there was no victim; those records were sealed without an application.
answers.citation: ORS 475C.397 and ORS 137.222, per the Oregon Judicial Department’s marijuana set-aside motion form (July 2023)

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: An adult may deliver up to 1 ounce of usable marijuana at a time to another adult 21 or older for noncommercial purposes.
answers.citation: ORS 475C.305(7) (2025 edition)

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Pennsylvania has no adult-use law. Without a medical card, possessing up to 30 grams of marijuana or 8 grams of hashish is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 30 days in jail, a fine of up to $500, or both.
answers.citation: Controlled Substance, Drug, Device and Cosmetic Act (Act 64 of 1972)

answers.question: driving
answers.short: Any amount in the blood is DUI
answers.detail: Driving with any amount of a Schedule I controlled substance or its metabolite in the blood is DUI, impaired or not. Marijuana is Schedule I under state law, and there is no exception for medical patients.

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: An employer may not fire, refuse to hire or otherwise discriminate against someone solely because they are certified to use medical marijuana. Employers need not allow use at work and may discipline employees for being under the influence at work when their conduct falls below the standard of care for the job.
answers.citation: Medical Marijuana Act (Act 16 of 2016), section 2103(b)

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Only grower/processors permitted by the Department of Health may grow medical marijuana. Pennsylvania has no adult-use home-grow law.
answers.citation: Medical Marijuana Act (Act 16 of 2016)

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Medical use is lawful only for a registered patient or caregiver with a Department of Health ID card and practitioner certification. A dispensary may sell no more than a 90-day supply, and smoking medical marijuana is unlawful.
answers.citation: Medical Marijuana Act (Act 16 of 2016)

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: Clean Slate limits access to (seals) certain records automatically: charges that did not end in a conviction; summary convictions after five years; and second- and third-degree misdemeanors and misdemeanors punishable by up to two years after seven years free of convictions punishable by a year or more. Court-ordered restitution must be paid. A pardon is a separate step. The law covers criminal records in general, not only cannabis cases; whether one record qualifies depends on the full record and the exclusions in the statute.
answers.citation: 18 Pa.C.S. § 9122.2, as amended by Act 36 of 2023

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adult use has been legal since December 1, 2022 for people at least 21 years old.
answers.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Licensed compassion centers are the retail stores currently selling adult-use cannabis.
answers.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: The law does not permit operating a vehicle, boat or aircraft under the influence of cannabis. Metabolites in a person’s system do not by themselves mean the person is under the influence.

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: An employer may not fire or discipline an employee solely for private, lawful cannabis use outside the workplace, as long as the employee has not worked and is not working under the influence. The rule gives way to a collective bargaining agreement that prohibits such use, and to federal contractors that would lose a federal benefit. For jobs that are hazardous, dangerous or essential to public welfare and safety, an employer may bar use in the 24 hours before a shift. Employers may act on a violation of a workplace drug policy or on working under the influence.
answers.citation: R.I. Gen. Laws § 21-28.11-29(d) and (e)

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to three mature and three immature plants.
answers.citation: Rhode Island Department of Health, Cannabis information for adults

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Cannabis Control Commission regulates both adult-use and medical marijuana.
answers.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may carry up to 1 ounce of flower, or the equivalent in concentrate, and keep up to 10 ounces at home.
answers.citation: Rhode Island Department of Health, Cannabis information for adults

answers.question: public-use
answers.short: No smoking or vaping in public
answers.detail: State law does not authorize smoking or vaping cannabis in any public place, and both are banned wherever smoking or vaping tobacco is banned.

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The Rhode Island Judiciary says the Rhode Island Cannabis Act of 2022 requires the courts to expunge eligible cases and charges automatically, at no cost. Under the Supreme Court’s Executive Order 2023-02 that covers criminal convictions for marijuana possession by people 18 and over and civil violations by people 21 and over, and not other marijuana convictions such as selling, delivering or manufacturing. Cases where possession was the only charge were cleared before April 30, 2023; the Judiciary said cases with other charges were on track for July 1, 2024. A person can check the Judiciary’s Public Portal, where an expunged case no longer appears, and can ask the court that heard the case to act sooner by filing a Notice for Expedited Marijuana Possession Expungement.
answers.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Act (2022) and Supreme Court Executive Order 2023-02, per the Rhode Island Judiciary’s release on phase one of marijuana expungement

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults may give away up to 1 ounce of cannabis, or the equivalent in concentrate, to another adult 21 or older without payment, as long as the transfer is not advertised or promoted.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: South Carolina has no adult-use law. A first offense for 1 ounce or less is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 30 days in jail or a fine of $100 to $200. A second or later offense can bring up to a year in jail or a fine of at least $200.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: State law excludes from the definition of marijuana a cannabidiol product with no more than 0.9% THC and more than 15% CBD, for a person with severe epilepsy, such as Lennox-Gastaut or Dravet syndrome, who has a written certification from a South Carolina-licensed physician.
answers.citation: S.C. Code 44-53-110 (definition of marijuana)

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: South Dakota has no adult-use law. The state Health Department says any sale or purchase of cannabis outside licensed medical cannabis establishments is illegal. Possessing 2 ounces or less is a Class 1 misdemeanor (up to one year in county jail, a fine of up to $2,000, or both), as Legislative Research Council staff summarized the law in 2021; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: SDCL 22-42-6, per Legislative Research Council staff (2021); South Dakota Department of Health; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists South Dakota as giving registered patients the same rights as people prescribed medication in dealings with an employer and in drug testing. Its chart says the protections yield to federal obligations and that employers may act on a positive test for safety-sensitive jobs. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: SDCL §§ 34-20G-22 and 34-20G-23, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Patients get a medical cannabis card, and the Department of Health certifies dispensaries.
answers.citation: South Dakota Department of Health, Medical cannabis

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Tennessee has no adult-use law. The Attorney General’s 2016 opinion describes possessing any amount as a Class A misdemeanor (up to 11 months and 29 days in jail, a fine of up to $2,500, or both), with minimum fines starting at $250. National compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Tenn. Code Ann. 39-17-418, per Attorney General Opinion 16-40; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: DISA’s national map lists Tennessee as CBD oil only, marked as legislation passed with a future effective date.
answers.citation: DISA national map

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Texas has no adult-use law. Possessing under 2 ounces of marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor, punishable by jail time and fines. That is how the Senate Research Center described state law in March 2025; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Tex. Health & Safety Code 481.121, per the Senate Research Center analysis of S.B. 1059 (2025); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: The Department of Public Safety runs the Compassionate Use Program created by the 2015 Texas Compassionate Use Act. DISA’s national map lists Texas as CBD oil only.
answers.citation: Texas Department of Public Safety; DISA national map

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Utah has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a class B misdemeanor, and a third conviction within seven years is a class A misdemeanor. That is the law as reprinted in a January 2026 House bill; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Utah Code 58-37-8(2)(d), as reprinted in 2026 H.B. 253; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: employment
answers.short: Public employees who are medical patients
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Utah as protecting state and local government employees only: their medical cannabis use is treated like a prescribed controlled substance, and a cardholder may not be retaliated against for a failed drug test without evidence of impairment. Its chart lists exceptions tied to federal funding, clearances and licenses. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Utah Code § 26-61a-111, as cited in the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Utah’s Center for Medical Cannabis works to give Utahns safe access to medical cannabis, and its site lists pharmacies that serve patients.
answers.citation: Utah Center for Medical Cannabis

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 2 ounces outside their home and generally may use cannabis in private residences.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Non-medical sales are currently illegal. Retail sales begin July 1, 2027.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority

answers.question: driving
answers.short: No impaired driving or use in a vehicle
answers.detail: It is illegal to drive under the influence of marijuana, or to use it while driving or riding as a passenger.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: Virginia’s Cannabis Control Authority says workplaces and employers may still prohibit cannabis use by their employees and enforce drug testing, and that Virginia law protects some medical cannabis use from employment action, though perhaps not for every medical user. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists that protection as covering employees who use cannabis oil under a valid written certification, with exceptions for impairment or possession at work, federal law and some defense-industry employers (Va. Code § 40.1-27.4); that part is not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions; Va. Code § 40.1-27.4, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Four plants per household, not per person, under specified requirements.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Virginia runs a medical cannabis program.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 2 ounces outside their private residence.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Consuming cannabis in any public place is illegal, as is using it while driving or riding as a passenger.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Virginia as automatically shielding misdemeanor cannabis convictions from public inspection. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may transfer 2 ounces or less to another adult without payment. Gifts tied to a sale or another exchange do not count.
answers.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older with a valid government-issued photo ID may buy cannabis.
answers.citation: Vermont Cannabis Control Board, Frequently asked questions

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Cannabis may only be bought legally from a licensed retailer or an integrated licensee’s retail arm. Since July 1, 2026, a retailer may sell up to 2 ounces, or the equivalent in products, in a single transaction to a buyer 21 or older with valid photo ID.
answers.citation: Vermont Cannabis Control Board, Frequently asked questions; 7 V.S.A. § 907(b), as amended by Act 176 (2026)

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: The adult-use law does not protect anyone from arrest or prosecution for operating a vehicle under the influence of cannabis or for consuming cannabis while operating a motor vehicle.

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Vermont as protecting patients through 2018 Attorney General guidance, not the medical cannabis law: a patient with a disability is protected under the state’s Fair Employment Practices Act. Its chart adds that a separate state law restricts drug testing. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Vermont Attorney General guidance (2018); Fair Employment Practices Act, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Adults may grow up to two mature and four immature plants, and a dwelling unit may have no more than that however many adults live there. Plants must be in an area screened from public view, with access limited to the grower and adults 21 or older who have the grower’s permission.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Vermont has a medical cannabis program.
answers.citation: Vermont Cannabis Control Board

answers.question: possession
answers.detail: Since July 1, 2026, adults 21 and older may possess up to 2 ounces of cannabis or 10 grams of hashish. Cannabis grown and stored at home under the home-grow rules does not count toward the limit.
answers.citation: 18 V.S.A. § 4230a, as amended by Act 176 (2026)

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: Consuming cannabis in any form in a public place is prohibited, with civil penalties of up to $100 for a first offense.
answers.citation: 7 V.S.A. § 833; Vermont Cannabis Control Board, Public safety and education questions

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Vermont as requiring automatic expungement, by January 1, 2022, of records involving up to two ounces of cannabis, 10 grams of hashish, four mature plants and eight immature plants. Its table says expungement and sealing by petition is available for other offenses after a waiting period. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: Up to 1 oz or 5 g hashish, not advertised
answers.detail: An adult 21 or older may dispense up to 1 ounce of cannabis or 5 grams of hashish to another adult 21 or older, as long as it is not advertised or promoted to the public. Unlawful sales are a crime.

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Only adults 21 and older can buy and possess cannabis.
answers.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

answers.question: buying
answers.detail: Cannabis can only be sold and bought at state-licensed retail stores, with valid photo ID. Adults may buy up to 1 ounce of usable cannabis, 16 ounces of solid edibles, 72 ounces in liquid form and 7 grams of concentrates.
answers.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

answers.question: driving
answers.detail: Driving with more than 5 nanograms of active THC per milliliter of blood is illegal.
answers.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: Since January 1, 2024, it is unlawful for an employer to discriminate in initial hiring because of a person’s use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace, or because an employer-required drug test finds non-psychoactive cannabis metabolites. The law covers initial hiring only: it does not apply to testing after hiring, such as post-accident or suspicion-based testing, and it leaves drug-free workplace rules in place. It does not cover applicants for jobs that need a federal background investigation or security clearance, jobs with law enforcement agencies and fire departments, other first responders, corrections officers, airline and aerospace jobs, or safety-sensitive jobs the employer identified in advance.

answers.question: home-grow
answers.detail: Washington does not allow home growing unless you are a qualified medical patient or designated provider with a valid authorization. Growing plants without one is a class C felony; a 2026 bill to allow adult home grows did not pass.
answers.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Growing cannabis at home; House bill report on HB 1449 (2025); SB 6204 bill summary

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: With a health care practitioner’s authorization, an adult patient may grow up to four plants. A recognition card from a medically endorsed store adds tax exemptions and higher limits: by default up to 3 ounces of usable cannabis (or equivalent products) and six plants. Patients 18 to 20 must register to buy.
answers.citation: Washington State Department of Health; RCW 69.51A.210

answers.question: possession
answers.short: 1 oz, 16 oz solid edibles, 72 oz liquid, 7 g conc.
answers.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy and possess up to 1 ounce of usable cannabis, 16 ounces of solid edibles, 72 ounces of drinks and 7 grams of concentrate.
answers.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Using and having cannabis

answers.question: public-use
answers.detail: It is illegal to consume cannabis in view of the public.
answers.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

answers.question: record-relief
answers.detail: Washington’s courts say the law does not vacate a conviction automatically: a person files a petition (form CrRLJ 09.0800) under RCW 9.96.060, gives the prosecutor a copy the same day and attends a hearing. A court will vacate a misdemeanor cannabis conviction if the person was 21 or older at the time of the offense; eligible offenses include those under RCW 69.50.4014 from July 1, 2004, under RCW 69.50.401(e) or (d) from May 21, 1971 to July 1, 2004, and under equivalent local ordinances. After vacation a person may state on job or housing applications that they were never convicted of that crime.
answers.citation: RCW 9.96.060, per the Washington Courts’ Instructions for Vacating Misdemeanor and Gross Misdemeanor Convictions (CrRLJ 09.0300, July 2022)

answers.question: sharing
answers.short: Up to 1/2 oz flower a day, free
answers.detail: In any 24-hour period, an adult may give another adult 21 or older up to half an ounce of usable cannabis or 8 ounces of solid edibles, with separate limits for other products, with no payment involved. The handoff must take place out of public view in a nonpublic place, or the product must be in its original store packaging.
answers.citation: RCW 69.50.4013(4), as reprinted in 2026 Senate Bill 6204; House bill report on HB 1449 (2025)

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Wisconsin has no adult-use law. A first conviction for possession is a misdemeanor (a fine of up to $1,000, up to six months in jail, or both), and a repeat conviction is a Class I felony. That is the Legislative Reference Bureau’s December 2023 summary of current law; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
answers.citation: Wis. Stat. 961.41(3g)(e), per Legislative Reference Bureau analysis; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: State law lets a person possess a cannabidiol product with a certification from a Wisconsin-licensed physician, issued within the past year, stating that it treats a medical condition.
answers.citation: Wis. Stat. 961.32(2m)

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: West Virginia has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a misdemeanor punishable by 90 days to 6 months in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. A first offense involving less than 15 grams must be handled through conditional discharge, under which completing probation ends the case without a conviction.

answers.question: employment
answers.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists West Virginia as barring employers from discharging, refusing to hire or discriminating against a person solely for being certified to use medical cannabis, with an exception for federal law. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
answers.citation: W. Va. Code § 16A-15-4, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Patients apply to the Office of Medical Cannabis for a card, and its site lists dispensaries.
answers.citation: West Virginia Office of Medical Cannabis

answers.question: adult-use
answers.detail: Wyoming has no adult-use law. Possessing up to 3 ounces of marijuana in plant form is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 12 months in jail, a $1,000 fine, or both. Larger amounts are a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison, a $10,000 fine, or both.

answers.question: medical
answers.detail: Wyoming law bars practitioners from prescribing or dispensing marijuana or THC except FDA-approved drugs such as dronabinol. Its former article on supervised medical use of hemp extracts (W.S. 35-7-1901 to 35-7-1903) was repealed in 2019, and hemp products are now outside the controlled substances law.
